newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan's Yasuda Trust to strengthen ties with Fuji.
newsitem.headline: Japan's Yasuda Trust to strengthen ties with Fuji.

text.p: Financially weak Yasuda Trust & Banking Co Ltd, Japan's fourth biggest trust bank, said on Wednesday it may issue subordinated bonds to its group firms, including Fuji Bank Ltd, to help bolster its capital base.
The bonds, worth about 30 billion yen ($260 million), are likely to be issued in the third quarter to Yasuda Mutual Life Insurance Co and Marubeni Corp as well as Fuji.

A bank spokesman denied a newspaper report that the bond issue is a prelude to establishing a financial holding company with its group institutions, but said it plans to strengthen business cooperation with the group companies, he also said.
Analysts said that the move to issue the bonds was aimed at boosting financially weak Yasuda Trust's capital base.

Fuji Bank and Yasuda Trust belong to the same Fuyo group, one of Japan's six major groups of companies. Firms belonging to the same groups are generally linked by cross-shareholdings and long-term business ties.
"The bond issue looks like Yasuda Trust is trying to avoid the downgrading by strengthening its capital base," said Yoshinobu Yamada, an analyst at Merrill Lynch Japan Inc.
He said that it is possible that Fuji and Yasuda Trust will form a financial holding company eventually.
On May 16, U.S. rating agency Standard & Poor's Corp announced that it placed the bank's debt ratings on its CreditWatch with negative implications.
The action reflects its concern about Yasuda's future performance in the face of "Big Bang" financial reforms and the bank's lingering asset-quality problems, it said.
Japanese banks are all re-examining their operational strategies in the face of the Big Bang deregulations.

If there is a large gap in the size of assets between a commercial and a trust bank and their customer base is different, it is likely some will choose to convert into holding-company structures, he said.
Another analyst, who declined to be named, said that Yasuda Trust has needed to boost its capital base by offering preferred stock or subordinated debt.
However, the stock market outlook makes it difficult for financially weak firms to float new issues in the market.
Life insurers, traditionally major buyers of subordinated bonds, are increasingly cost- and risk-conscious.
That has forced Yasuda Trust to ask its group companies to buy the subordinated bonds, the analyst said.
He also said that he did not expect the marriage between Fuji and Yasuda Trust anytime soon as Yasuda Trust needs to be slimmer and dispose of problem loans on its own at first.

Competition in the trust business will grow due to deregulation and only two big trust banks -- Mitsubishi Trust & Banking Corp and Sumitomo Trust & Banking Co Ltd -- are expected to survive, analysts said.

Trust banks engage in both ordinary banking and trust business in which they are allowed to manage investors' funds. Under the "Big Bang" reforms too boost competition, however, Japan is to break down barriers between highly segmented banking sectors as well as the barriers between banks, brokers and insurers.

As a part of the reforms, Japan parliament passed a bill last month lifting a decades-old ban on holding companies -- firms which control one or more other firms but do not themselves engage in a specific business.
Following the passage, the Finance Ministry is expected to submit another bill legalising financial holding companies in a special session of parliament this autumn.

Japanese banks are interested in financial holding companies because the corporate structure of such firms gives them more flexible management by setting different pay scales and cutting unprofitable operations, analysts said.

However, they said that it may take some time to see the first financial holding company as Japan has not yet made a final decision on tax changes, a major factor in deciding whether to set up holding companies. ($1=115 yen)
